blocks.text: Population survivorship is the percentage of a group alive at a given age, shown by survivorship curves with survivors on the y-axis and age on the x-axis.

blocks.caption: Three survivorship curves
rows: most live to old age, then die quickly; environment has little effect
constant chance of death throughout life
very high death rate of the young; adults survive much better

blocks.alt: A graph of number of survivors (log scale 0.1, 1, 10, 100) against age (1, 3, 5). Type I (convex), red, stays high and falls steeply near the end. Type II (diagonal), blue, is a straight line from top left to bottom right. Type III (concave), orange, falls steeply at once and then levels off near the bottom.
blocks.caption: Figure 25.7: Survivorship curves (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 25.7).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 25.7 labels the foot of its logarithmic survivor axis '0'; a log scale cannot reach 0, and the step below 1 is 0.1, as drawn above.

Population growth is the increase in the number of individuals over a period of time. In the exponential model a population grows without limit at its maximum rate, by the same ratio per unit time; not all populations show it. In the logistic model the population eventually meets limits, shortages of space, light, water or nutrients, and stabilises at the carrying capacity of its habitat, giving an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve.

blocks.alt: One graph of population size (0 to 1250) against number of generations (0 to 15). Two curves start together near generation 4. Exponential growth (pink, J shape) climbs ever faster past 1000 by about generation 8.5. Logistic growth (blue, S shape) slows and levels off at the carrying capacity, about 750.
blocks.caption: Figure 25.8: Population growth models (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 25.8).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 25.8 titles its y-axis 'Population sze'; it should read 'Population size', as drawn above.

Population density is the number of individuals per unit area or volume, such as the number of mulberry trees per square kilometre in Muzaffarabad or of E. coli per millilitre in a test tube. Near the carrying capacity, high density means severe competition, fewer births, more deaths and more pollution.

items: Random spacing: individuals do not interact strongly; uncommon, seen in some plants whose wind-dispersed seeds grow wherever they fall.
Uniform spacing: individuals evenly spaced, as when plants inhibit nearby growth or animals such as nesting penguins keep territories.
Clumped spacing: individuals in groups or clusters, because resources are patchy or animals live in groups; common in nature, seen in plants that drop seeds straight down.

blocks.text: 5. Carrying capacity and 6. minimum viable population

The carrying capacity is the largest number of individuals of a species that an environment can support sustainably over a long period, set by limiting factors such as food, water, shelter and nesting sites, and by predators and diseases. The minimum viable population size is the smallest number needed for a population to persist; below it the risk of extinction is high, because inbreeding weakens the population and its immunity (as in the few remaining Himalayan brown bears of Pakistan) and a single flood or forest fire could wipe it out.

blocks.title: Day of Eight Billion
blocks.text: The world population took 12 years to grow from 7 to 8 billion, reaching 8 billion in 2022. It will take about 15 years (to 2037) to reach 9 billion, and by 2050 it will be nearly 10 billion, mostly in developing regions.
